# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
The comment's documentary findings are valuable and, as far as I can check, correct. **Its central conclusion, that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact," is not supported by its own analysis.** Its corrected estimate is still +10.8%. The step from there to zero rests on a weak novelty argument, and the comment uses the Varden trial selectively.

## Arithmetic check

Most figures are correct:

- **Hours ratios.** 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 (−14.1%) and 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 (−13.9%).
- **Table 2.** 95.1 / 0.8 = +18.9%; 98.4 / 0.859 = +14.6%; 95.4 / 0.861 = +10.8%. All match.
- **Revenue.** 1.014 / 1.041 = 0.974, a real fall of 2.6%.

Two figures don't hold:

- **The hours decomposition doesn't add up.** Section 3 gives two sources of extra time: +0.7 hours per day on four days (2.8 hours) and 1.6 hours on the day off. That is 4.4 hours above the 32-hour schedule, or about 36.4 hours. The reported pilot figure is 34.6, only 2.6 hours above schedule. Perhaps the averages cover different groups, such as the 1.6 hours applying only to staff who worked on their day off. Either way, the figures need reconciling.
- **"Around month ten" is wrong on its own terms.** A straight line through 0.61 SD at month 3 and 0.29 at month 6 falls about 0.107 per month and reaches zero at about month 8.7, not 10.

## What the comment does well

- **Attrition.** Section 1 documents that seven of the nine withdrawals happened *after* the reduced schedule began, and that six cited workload or output. That directly contradicts the working paper's "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." This is the comment's most important finding, and Halden's authors should be asked to respond to it.
- **Records versus manager ratings.** Comparing manager ratings with organisations' own records within the same 23 organisations is a clean test. The finding is a 3.8-point gap, with managers' figures higher in 19 of 23 cases.
- **Actual hours.** Using time-tracking data puts the actual reduction at about 14% rather than 20%.
- **Revenue.** Adjusting revenue for inflation shows a real fall.
- **Sector claims.** Section 5 correctly identifies the per-hour "gain in every sector" as produced by dividing by 0.8.
- **Data note.** It candidly says the corrected estimates describe non-random subsets.

## 1. The conclusion contradicts the evidence presented

After correcting output and hours, the comment's best estimate is +10.8% output per actual hour. It then moves to "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty" on three grounds:

- **Selection was never corrected.** The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems, which includes attrition. Table 2 corrects only output measurement and hours; attrition is never adjusted for or bounded.
- **Novelty is asserted, not measured** (see section 2 below).
- **There is no CI for the 10.8%.** With 17 organisations, readers can't tell whether it is distinguishable from zero. If it isn't, the defensible conclusion is that the evidence can't distinguish a modest gain from none. That is different from saying the gain is entirely an artifact.

The phrase "in our assessment" softens the tone but does not close this gap. The Data note's own caveat (the subsets "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole") also undercuts the generalisation to "reduced-hours schemes" in general.

## 2. The novelty argument doesn't test the right outcome

- **It uses energy as a proxy for output.** The claim concerns output per hour, but the evidence is a self-reported energy scale. Falling energy doesn't show falling productivity.
- **The direct test was available but not reported.** The pilot collected the output index *monthly*. With the microdata, the authors could show whether output per hour declined from month 1 to month 6 in the 17 well-measured organisations. If it did, that is strong evidence for novelty. If it didn't, the novelty account is much weaker. Either way it belongs in the comment.
- **Extrapolating a straight line from two points is not justified.** A decaying effect may level off above zero instead of reaching it. Even on the comment's own extrapolation, the zero point is about month 9, not 10.
- **"Burden of proof" settles nothing.** Six months being too short to tell novelty from a durable effect is a reason for uncertainty, not a reason to conclude the effect is zero.

## 3. The Varden trial is cited selectively

The comment calls Varden's counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature" but doesn't mention Varden's other stratum:

- **Case-processing results.** Varden's case-processing offices showed +12.5% output per actual hour at nine months, with output per employee about unchanged (−2.1%, CI −6.8 to +2.6).
- **Varden avoids the problems the comment identifies.** It used randomisation (no self-selection), record-based output, actual hours from timesheets, and no attrition problem.
- **The two estimates are close.** Varden's 12.5% is close to the comment's corrected 10.8% for Halden, from a design that rules out the comment's selection and measurement explanations.

Varden's estimate has its own weaknesses: few clusters, a possible novelty effect in the treatment arm, and part of the gain likely coming from cut meetings. Even so, it contradicts "entirely an artifact," and the comment should address it. In addition:

- **The counter stratum also showed a per-hour gain** (+6.7%), although as I noted in my review of Varden, that gain mostly reflects higher utilisation as queues lengthened.
- **"Where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output" needs qualifying.** It holds when the same staff cover unchanged opening hours with no extra hiring, which is how Varden ran it. The comment should frame it that way, as a result of that staffing choice.

## 4. Attrition can't account for "most of" the gain

The new attrition evidence is important, but its size matters. Nine of 70 organisations withdrew, about 13%. For the 70-organisation average per-hour gain to fall from 10.8% to zero, the nine withdrawals would need an average change of about −73% (10.8 × 61 / 9). That figure is unweighted, but no reasonable weighting makes it plausible.

Attrition bias is real but probably worth a few points, not the whole effect. The comment should bound it, for example using the withdrawn organisations' early monthly outputs if those exist in the microdata, or with worst-case bounds. As it stands, the comment lists attrition among problems that "account for most of the reported gain" without estimating its contribution.

## 5. Table 2 mixes subsets with corrections

The four rows use different samples: 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. The fall from 23.4% to 10.8% therefore mixes two things: the effect of each correction, and differences between subsets. All four specifications should be reported on the same 17 organisations, from manager-reported output with scheduled hours through to record-based output with actual hours. That would show how much each correction contributes.

Two related points:

- **Weighting.** State whether means are employee-weighted, as in Halden. If they aren't, 98.9 and 98.7 aren't directly comparable.
- **Are records the right benchmark?** For professional services, "billable hours delivered" is closer to an input than an output. Records are better than manager impressions, but the comment treats them as correct without question.

## 6. The meetings section attacks a claim Varden didn't make

The Varden authors said explicitly that their meetings analysis was unregistered, rested on seven offices, "cannot establish a mechanism," and would be tested in a registered confirmatory analysis. The comment's warning that it "should not be cited as a mechanism" therefore argues against a claim Varden didn't make. The description "selected for analysis after the results were known" also doesn't match Varden's account: calendar data were collected in month six at managers' request.

The comment also misses two things:

- **The between-arm comparison is stronger than the correlation.** The meeting-hours gap (3.8 vs 7.1 hours) compares randomised arms, which is stronger evidence than the r = 0.71 within one arm. Its weakness is that no baseline was measured.
- **It cuts against the comment's own thesis.** If cutting low-value meetings produces part of the gain, that is a genuine efficiency gain, not an artifact.

## 7. Abstract errors

- **Revenue doesn't affect the per-hour figure.** The abstract counts unadjusted revenue among four problems that "account for most of the reported gain." But revenue plays no part in the per-hour calculation. It belongs to a separate criticism of Halden's secondary claims.
- **Attrition wasn't corrected.** "Correcting the first three" is inaccurate, as noted in section 1 above.

## Smaller points

- **Choice of price index.** CPI may not be the right deflator for organisations' revenue; sector or producer prices would fit better. Real revenue also needs a sector benchmark before it says anything about the pilot.
- **Small retail sample.** The record-based retail figure (−11.2%) rests on three organisations and should be flagged as such.
- **The meetings section is out of scope.** The comment re-analyses Halden, but Section 7 critiques Varden, so its relevance to the comment's argument needs explaining.

## Overall

The comment makes a real contribution. It shows that Halden's headline is overstated by more than half, documents misreported attrition, and supports criticisms made of the working paper (including mine) with microdata. The supportable conclusion is roughly this: correcting for measurement roughly halves the gain; attrition and novelty may reduce it further by amounts not yet estimated; and randomised evidence from Varden suggests a real but modest per-hour gain in backlog work, with a loss of service in coverage-bound work without extra staff. "Entirely an artifact" goes beyond what the comment's own data and the literature it cites can support.
